mission_1.search: On the open map, BFS and A* both found the same shortest path of 13.5 meters. However, BFS expanded 928 nodes, while A* expanded only 700. This means A* examined 228 fewer cells. In my code, BFS uses a queue to explore cells in the order they are discovered, without considering how close they are to the goal. A* uses the Manhattan distance heuristic along with the cost traveled so far to prioritize cells that seem closer to the goal. This helps A* explore fewer cells while still finding the same shortest path.
mission_1.failure:
On the constrained map, BFS found the shortest path of 24.5 meters and expanded 848 nodes. DFS expanded fewer nodes (448), but its path was much longer at 50 meters. This is because my DFS uses a stack and explores one direction deeply instead of finding the shortest route. IDDFS reached the resource limit after 250,001 expansions because it repeatedly searches with increasing depth limits, causing it to revisit many cells.
For the unreachable case, all four algorithms (BFS, DFS, IDDFS, and A*) returned **no_path**. This means they finished searching and confirmed that no valid path existed. In contrast, **resource_limit** means the algorithm stopped because it exceeded the allowed number of expansions or time, not because the goal was impossible to reach.
I used AI to help implement and understand the algorithms. I checked the code myself by running the small tests and full evaluation, comparing the results, and checking that the algorithms returned valid paths or appropriate failure statuses.
